newsitem.title: MEXICO: Was vote death knell for Mexico's long-ruling PRI?.
newsitem.headline: Was vote death knell for Mexico's long-ruling PRI?.

text.p: Mexico's opposition celebrated historic gains on Tuesday, saying the death knell had been sounded for the ruling party after its 68 years in power.

Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo agreed there had been an electoral funeral on Sunday, but he said it was for Mexico's one-party system and not the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has ruled since it was founded in 1929.
"After these elections, no one can call the PRI Mexico's only party, the party of state or an appendage of government," Zedillo said.

Mexicans handed the PRI a stinging loss on Sunday, probably removing its majority in the lower house of Congress for the first time and voting in an opposition leftist as the first elected mayor of Mexico City.
"The PRI is in terminal condition," Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, leader of the left-leaning Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD), told reporters.
"Look at it: The PRI falls, the Mexican Stock Exchange goes up. That shows all that Mexico really needed was democracy," said the leader of the PRD, which made strong gains in the election.

Mexican stocks rallied 1.69 percent on the Mexican Bolsa on Tuesday to close at a record high. Dealers said investors were pleased the elections went peacefully and Mexico appeared well on its way to full democracy.
Voters repeatedly said they wanted change after decades of the PRI, an economic crisis following the bungled devaluation of the peso in December 1994 and a string of corruption scandals.
Analysts said it was too early to tell if the elections meant the PRI and the one-party system it spawned really were dying or if the PRI was changing only enough to continue its hold on power.

"(The elections) were a very important step but by no means definitive. There is always the possibility of a retreat or a return to the bad old habits of the past," Mario Vargas Llosa, a well-known Peruvian novelist, told Mexican radio.
Vargas Llosa caused an uproar a few years ago when he described the PRI as the "perfect dictatorship," because it kept absolute power beneath a facade of regular elections and apparent democracy.
But observers agreed that Mexico did wake up this week as a more democratic and pluralistic nation.
"The clearest winner in all of this was society," Miguel Angel Granados Chapa, a columnist for the Reforma newspaper, said on Tuesday.
Zedillo said the PRI was still the largest single political party in Mexico despite its probable loss of majority control of the lower house of Congress to the opposition.
Preliminary results for Congress, with 86.84 percent of the vote counted on Tuesday, showed the PRI winning 38.86 percent of the national vote.
It was followed by 27 percent for the conservative National Action Party (PAN) and 25.6 percent for the left-wing PRD.
The PRI would need 42 percent of the national vote to retain control of the lower house. In the last congressional race, in 1994, it got 50.2 percent.
In the Mexico City race, veteran leftist Cuauhtemoc Cardenas trounced his PRI and PAN opponents by a 2-to-1 margin.
